prompt: A new fraud-analysis team wants to start consuming order events and, on day one, process the **last 7 days of history** before continuing live. Events currently flow through SNS standard topics fanned out to SQS queues. What is the most important constraint they face?

options.text: A new SQS subscription only receives messages published after it was created, so history must come from elsewhere
options.explanation: Correct. SNS does not retain messages for future subscribers (outside the separate SNS FIFO archive and replay feature). In a log such as Kafka, a new consumer group could just start from the earliest retained offset.

options.text: SNS FIFO topics are required before any new subscriber can be added
options.explanation: Wrong. New subscriptions can be added to standard topics at any time. FIFO is about ordering, not about adding subscribers.

options.text: The fraud team must share an existing queue with billing to see past messages
options.explanation: Wrong. Sharing a queue makes the teams competing consumers, so each would see only some of the messages, and messages already processed by billing were deleted.

options.text: SQS cannot hold 7 days of messages
options.explanation: Wrong. SQS retention can be set up to 14 days. The problem is not how long the new queue can hold messages but that messages published before it existed were never delivered to it.

workedExample:
1. In SNS + SQS, copies are made **at publish time**, only into subscriptions that exist then.
2. Each copy is deleted from its queue once that subscriber acknowledges it.
3. So there is no shared history for a newcomer to read.
4. Options for the fraud team:
   - Backfill from the source database or a data lake.
   - Use SNS FIFO's archive and replay, if the topic is FIFO and archiving was enabled beforehand.
   - Longer term, put events on a retained log (Kafka, Kinesis) where a new consumer group can start from `earliest`.

This replayability is one of the strongest reasons teams adopt log-based streaming.

prompt: An SNS topic receives a steady stream of orders and fans out to 6 SQS queues. Each queue's consumers currently receive and delete one message per API call. Six more teams now want their own subscriptions. Assuming no retries or empty polls, which prediction about consumer-side SQS API calls is right?

options.text: Unchanged, because SNS still receives each order only once
options.explanation: Wrong. SNS is published to once, but it delivers a separate copy into every subscribed queue. Each copy must be received and deleted by that queue's consumers, so consumer-side traffic scales with the number of subscriptions.

options.text: It doubles, and batching cannot help because every message still needs its own receive and delete
options.explanation: Wrong on batching. Each message must be received and deleted, but one ReceiveMessage or DeleteMessageBatch call can handle up to 10 messages, so full batches cut the number of calls roughly tenfold.

options.text: It grows about 36-fold, because each new subscription multiplies the existing ones
options.explanation: Wrong. Subscriptions add copies; they do not multiply each other. Twelve subscriptions mean twelve copies of each message, twice as many as six.

options.text: It doubles, because each new subscription receives and deletes its own copy; full batches of 10 could cut the total about tenfold
options.explanation: Correct. Consumer-side calls grow with the publish rate times the number of subscriptions, so going from 6 to 12 doubles them. Batching divides calls by the average batch size, so full batches of 10 bring the doubled total below today's unbatched level.

workedExample:
1. Each subscription needs its own delivered copy, and its workers receive and delete that copy independently.
2. Adding the same number of subscriptions again doubles those consumer operations under the stated assumptions.
3. Batching combines up to ten messages in one receive or batch-delete request, reducing API calls when batches fill.
4. Measure actual batch fill, empty polls and retries before estimating costs; publish and delivery charges are separate.

link.title: Fanout SNS notifications to SQS queues

prompt: An SNS **standard** topic fans out to three SQS standard queues (billing, shipping, email). Which statements about duplicates and ordering are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Because SNS assigns one MessageId per publish, at most one subscriber can ever receive a duplicate
options.explanation: Wrong. Delivery to each subscription is independent and at-least-once, so any or all of the subscribers can receive a copy more than once.

options.text: Each subscriber must deduplicate independently, keyed on a stable event ID
options.explanation: Correct. Each subscriber has its own processing and its own effects, so each needs its own record of what it has already applied.

options.text: A duplicate may reach billing while email receives the message exactly once
options.explanation: Correct. Retries and redeliveries happen per subscription and per queue, so subscribers can see different numbers of copies of the same event.

options.text: An SNS FIFO topic with SQS FIFO queues would give each subscriber ordering within a message group
options.explanation: Correct. SNS FIFO topics can fan out to SQS FIFO queues and preserve order (and deduplication) per message group for each subscription.

options.text: One shared deduplication record keyed only by event ID is sufficient for all three subscribers
options.explanation: Wrong. If billing records the event ID first, shipping and email would see it as already processed and skip their own work. Dedup state must be per subscriber, for example keyed on (subscriber, eventId).

workedExample:
1. Fan-out creates **independent** deliveries. Think of three separate at-least-once channels that share only a source.
2. So duplicates are per channel: billing might see 2 copies, shipping 1, email 1.
3. Therefore dedup is per subscriber. A shared table keyed only by event ID would suppress other subscribers. A shared table keyed by (subscriber, eventId) is valid; commit its record atomically with that subscriber's effects.
4. Ordering: standard SNS and SQS give none. If order within an entity matters, use SNS FIFO → SQS FIFO with `MessageGroupId = entityId`.

prompt: A company has two needs: (a) route about 50 business events per second between 40 internal services and SaaS integrations using content-based rules, and (b) ingest **400,000 clickstream events per second** that data scientists replay from the start whenever a model changes. Which combination fits best?

options.text: An event bus such as EventBridge for both
options.explanation: Wrong. An event bus is designed for integration at moderate volume. EventBridge supports archive/replay and adjustable quotas, so these are not impossible. Its routing model is a less direct fit than independently positioned log readers for this sustained replay-heavy workload; validate quotas and cost.

options.text: SNS + SQS for (b), with a new queue for each replay
options.explanation: Wrong. A new SQS subscription only receives messages published after it was created, so it cannot replay history at all.

options.text: Kafka for (a) and an event bus for (b)
options.explanation: Wrong. This is the wrong way round. Kafka could handle (a), but the event bus is the weak choice for the high-volume, replay-heavy stream.

options.text: An event bus for (a), and a retained log such as Kafka or Kinesis for (b)
options.explanation: Correct. Low-volume integration benefits from managed routing rules and built-in targets. High-throughput clickstream with replay needs a partitioned, retained log where each consumer group can start from the earliest offset.

workedExample:
Match each workload to the tool's strengths:

| Need | Volume | Replay? | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) integration | ~50/s | No | Event bus |
| (b) clickstream | 400k/s | Yes | Log |

1. (a) is about **routing**: many targets, content-based rules, low operational effort.
2. (b) is about **throughput and history**: append-only partitions, retention measured in days, consumers that rewind.
3. Ordinary SNS standard fan-out cannot rewind. SNS FIFO archive/replay is an explicit alternative if enabled in advance; it is not an independent consumer-offset log.
4. Using two tools is normal. Pick per workload, not one tool for everything.
